title: Wenceslaus (28 September)
hookLine: the good king of the carol was a duke, and his own brother had him killed

lines: A STORY THAT ENDS AT A CHURCH DOOR.
cards: Snow, deep and crisp and even.
A king looks out his window on the feast of Stephen, sees a poor man gathering firewood, and sets off through the storm with food and wine, his page stepping in his footprints to keep from freezing.
That's the Christmas carol, an English Victorian song written long after the man it names. The real Wenceslaus was not a king, and his story doesn't end at a warm table. It ends at a church door.

teach.h: A DUKE OF BOHEMIA, NOT A KING.
teach.b: Wenceslaus, Václav in Czech, was a duke of Bohemia, in the lands that are now the Czech Republic.

Tradition remembers him as a ruler who prayed, helped the poor, and tried to govern as a Christian when the court around him was split over the faith. His grandmother Ludmila, also honored as a saint, raised him in it.
Not everyone in the family was pleased.
His younger brother, Boleslaus, wanted power. The old accounts tell it this way: Boleslaus invited Wenceslaus to a feast.

The next morning, as Wenceslaus walked to Mass, his brother and his men attacked him at the door of the church, and he died there. Brother against brother, at the doorway to worship. It's a story as old as Genesis.
After Cain kills Abel, God asks him where his brother is, and Cain answers, in the Douay-Rheims: "Am I my brother's keeper?" In the Wenceslaus story, that old question comes back at a church door.
In time, people began to honor Wenceslaus as a martyr, and he became the patron of the Czech people. In Prague, a great square bears his name, with his statue on horseback at the top.
The carol calls him a king anyway: good king Wenceslas.

teach.h: A TITLE HE EARNED, NOT HELD.

teach.b: In the song, a title he earned.

how: Saint Wenceslaus is remembered on 28 September, a national feast in the Czech Republic; Catholics there keep it with Mass, and his statue in Prague's Wenceslas Square is a gathering place.

games.q: you're Wenceslaus. your brother invites you to a feast, though there's bad blood over who should rule. what do you do?
o: go, and keep walking to Mass in the morning
raise an army against him first
games.why: the old accounts say he went, and the next morning, on his way to Mass, he was attacked at the church door.

practice: Bring to mind a family that's split, yours or someone else's: siblings who don't speak, parents and children who can't be in the same room. Don't fix it; just hold both sides, without choosing a winner.
If you pray, name them before God and ask for one small thaw; if you don't, simply wish each of them a little peace.

wordCard.voice: Wenceslaus. A duke of Bohemia who governed as a Christian, was killed by his brother's men at a church door, and is remembered in a carol as the good king.

orig.note: his name in Czech; Wenceslaus is the Latin form used in the Church's calendar.

carryVoice: Your line: good king. The carol keeps him walking through the snow. One thousand twenty-nine days now.
